title: Does using AI to build a game prototype mean the game was “made by AI”?
author: DonkeyFar5962
selftext:
I got this comment on one of my videos:  
“Made by people like you” ❌ — “Made by AI” ✅

I understand where the criticism comes from, but I think it presents a false choice.

AI can shorten the distance between an idea and a playable prototype, but it still needs someone to choose the concept, shape the experience, make decisions and keep testing it.

I made this video as a response, but I’m genuinely interested in how other developers see it:

**At what point does using AI stop being a tool and start replacing the creator?**

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: Any AI use, made by AI. Really easy.

replies.author: hydrangers
replies.body: Which is literally every game out there at this point. No one who is actually releasing anything these days is not using AI in one form or another, especially large studios.

replies.author: Kingnorik
replies.body: I'm a full believer in AI game dev and have a fully AI game out on play store. It's disclosed as AI because I'm honest. If that makes people not want to play it that's fine, but I'm not ashamed and not a liar.

replies.author: hydrangers
replies.body:
I also have a game made using AI. It's hilarious to me because people will leave reviews saying things like "the game is awesome but I'm giving 3 stars because AI was used."

There are also people that leave 5 star reviews saying they think it's a great game and fun to play, but still have to voice their dislike of the use of AI to make it.

It's ridiculous.

replies.author: DonkeyFar5962
replies.body:
That's what made me to write this post. If you enjoyed the game, why should the tool used to create it affect the score? After all, a fun game is a fun game.

To me, it's a tool. Is a carpenter any less of a carpenter for using an electric screwdriver instead of a traditional one?

replies.author: jackadgery85
replies.body:
Yes when i take multiple photos, then spend hours in Photoshop retouching them and compositing them, if i use generative fill on 12 pixels, it's definitely made by AI. got it.

AI is also very good at knowing what's fun in a game that's right. Oh and i remembered that if i collect thousands of soil samples and design a research profile, and have ai analyse my samples, the research was done by AI. 

Thanks for clearing that up

replies.author: Kingnorik
replies.body: Maybe try changing the meaning of made with AI assistance to a positive one instead of being ashamed you used a tool. An either case tell people how it's made.

replies.author: jackadgery85
replies.body: I'm not ashamed at all lmao. I'm pointing out the stupidity of your comment

replies.author: DonkeyFar5962
replies.body: But is that necessarily a bad thing? If AI helps me create something beyond my abilities, why wouldn't I use it? Especially if the result is a fun game I can play and share with my friends.for me, AI is a tool that expands creative possibilities and democratizes access to skills and knowledge. why should that be considered a negative?

comments.author: lyeeedar
comments.body:
The only definition that matters is the one for Steam, and that is very clear.

You only have to declare if the art or music that is shown to the player is made with ai. Literally nothing else, not code, not prototypes, not concepts. Just if the thing the player sees art wise or hears music wise is ai does it require a declaration

replies.author: unfamily_friendly
replies.body:
Models and textst too. Basically, code is out of question, you can prompt all the logic. But everything else in a final product, be it images, sounds, music, 3d models, textures, fonts, texts, dialogues, localisation, promo materials on a steam page - must be disclosed

I think it's also important, that if you had AI generated stuff and didn't include it into a build - you shouldn't disclose it. A concept art and references can be made by AI, and you might look at them and draw manually. You don't need to disclose it. Generation inspiration song by AI, but making a final music in FL Studio (with no AI generated samples ofc) needs no disclosure too

replies.author: KHRZ
replies.body: What if code made the graphics and music?

replies.author: lyeeedar
replies.body: Unless you are embedding a neural net to generate it live it doesn't count. Steam is pretty clear that code does not count as ai , no matter the source that creates it

replies.author: KHRZ
replies.body: It's kind of a technicality though. The same pixels/vector graphics in formats like png/svg could be drawn by exactly equivalent code.

replies.author: lyeeedar
replies.body: Oh I fully agree. I'm just saying what steam defines, as they are the only authority on this a dev should care about (because they own the only game platform that actually brings value).

comments.author: Toastti
comments.body:
Well one tip is that it sure doesn't help when your entire response and post is fully AI generated text. If you want to sway someone and convince them a game is worthwhile even with AI helping create it you should at least put a human response to a comment like that 

Also you didn't link the response video.

replies.author: DonkeyFar5962
replies.body:
fair criticism. I did spend time shaping the argument and making the video, but I can see how the wording feels overly polished and impersonal.

My actual experience is that AI can get me to a playable prototype quickly, but most first versions aren’t particularly fun. Choosing the mechanics, testing them and deciding what to change is still where I feel most involved.

The link of the video is: [https://youtube.com/shorts/KenKA1vqZkQ?feature=share](https://youtube.com/shorts/KenKA1vqZkQ?feature=share)

comments.author: theEsel01
comments.body: If your prompt is "make me a viral steam game" yes - my opinion. If your prompt includes mechanics and a whole description of the design and mechanics, one could argue not... but thats just how I would approach that.

comments.author: waypostmaster
comments.body:
**tl;dr**: the extent to which human `selection, arrangement, skill, and judgment` went into the product is the more useful dimension to focus on, not whether one of the tools that was used to create the thing was "AI"   
  
Hmm, yes the game is made by AI. I think it's important to disclose that. In fact, I was quite clear at the outside: not one ounce of human coding expertise between the chair and keyboard, that's a promise. 

I think the more interesting question is the question of copyright in what the AI emits. If you created something that can be copyrighted, that it was made by you, because something created **solely** by AI cannot be copyrighted. I went over this a bit in the license section of [something](http://waypost.dev) I co-drafted with an AI agent, and yes- this text was also AI-assisted but fully human-driven with all the creativity, emotion, and chaos that humans bring:

>**On this document's own authorship — the keeper's position, stated as a position.** I dispute that there is no copyright in what I am making here. The law in both countries I live under denies protection to the machine's *unaided* output and to nothing else. In the United States the D.C. Circuit's rule is that the author must be a human — *the person who created, operated, or used* the system — and the Copyright Office has since registered a work on the strength of a human's documented selection and arrangement of machine output. In Canada, originality is *skill and judgement* (CCH), and whether an AI can stand as author is before the Federal Court now in *CIPPIC v. Sahni*, T-1717-24, where the registration under challenge names the tool as co-author — the claim this document declines to make. **My contribution is not three prompts. It is the direction, selection, correction and arrangement of every line here across hundreds of turns, and the record of that work is the git history and the logs this specification describes.** That is the authorial act the statutes protect, and it is what CC BY 4.0 above dedicates — a dedication presupposes something mine to give. The machine-emitted spans are contested ground; I do not claim them, and I do not concede them.

comments.author: mechatui
comments.body: If any art or music is built with AI then yes by steam standards. If it’s a typical AI clone one shot trying to get rich quick or get a few bucks game then people will call it AI

comments.author: Maleficent_Public621
comments.body:
I think this whole attitude comes from people who do not work in the software engineering space to begin with. I hate slop, and I hate vibe coding, but the fact of the matter is that modern software development is done with the assistance of AI. I don't really think this meaningfully replaces the developer. It just allows you to develop software without memorizing nuances and syntax of frameworks/languages, but does not substitute you as the system designer and author of the project itself. 

At work, most of the stuff that I do is planning and designing what the actual system looks like end to end, and firing up agents to implement them. I don't think this takes away from the fact that I shipped a feature.

This isn't unique to game dev, but the TLDR is engineers with good product instinct will float to the top.

comments.author: DocHolidayPhD
comments.body: I think it's where more decisions were made without a human involved than with...

comments.author: Morph_Games
comments.body:
You go to the baker and say "I want a chocolate cake with pink frosting and blue candies on top." The baker mixes the ingredients, bakes this cake, and decorates it. You pay the baker and take possession of the cake.

Did *you* make the cake?

replies.author: DonkeyFar5962
replies.body:
your analogy is valid if you simply tell the AI, “Make me a Tetris game,” and accept the first result it gives you. But it becomes less accurate when you test the game, iterate, give further instructions, and make decisions about its physics, visuals, mechanics and difficulty. At that point, you’re not just the customer. you’re also acting as the designer, director or producer

there’s another important difference: the baker is a person with their own intention, judgment and craft. AI has no independent creative intent. It generates from your direction, and you’re the one deciding whether the result works or what needs to change.

  
To me, AI is closer to a chisel that helps a sculptor shape an idea than another sculptor being commissioned to make the statue. It may be a far more powerful tool, but the direction, judgment and intent still come from the person using it.
